entities.summary:
Abu Talib Muhammad ibn Ali al-Makki (fl. 10th century) was a renowned hadith scholar, Shafi'i jurist, and Sufi mystic from Baghdad, whose comprehensive collection of hadith, Mu'jam al-Tawil, became a cornerstone of Sunni Islamic scholarship. Al-Makki's works were heavily influenced by his teacher, Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Hanbal, and his writings demonstrate a deep understanding of Shafi'i jurisprudence and Sufi mysticism. As a leading figure in the Shafi'i school of thought, al-Makki's teachings had a profound impact on the development of Islamic law and the arts of hadith scholarship. His legacy extends beyond the confines of Baghdad, as his works were studied and transmitted throughout the Islamic world, influencing scholars and thinkers across the Middle East, North Africa, and Central Asia. The Mu'jam al-Tawil remains a seminal work in the field of hadith studies, with its 100 volumes containing over 60,000 hadith narrations.

 Al-Makki's significance in the broader narrative of Islamic history cannot be overstated. His contributions to the development of Shafi'i jurisprudence and his role as a leading figure in the Sufi movement demonstrate a profound understanding of the complex interplay between Islamic theology, law, and mysticism. As a scholar and mystic, al-Makki's work embodies the ideals of Islamic scholarship and spiritual inquiry, inspiring generations of scholars and seekers of knowledge.

 The impact of al-Makki's work can be seen in the many scholars and thinkers who followed in his footsteps, including the famous Sufi mystic, Ibn Arabi, who often referenced al-Makki's works in his own writings. Al-Makki's influence can also be seen in the many institutions and centers of learning that he helped to establish, including the famous Madrasa al-Makkiyya in Baghdad, which became a hub of learning and scholarship for centuries to come.
